vignette: John, a 38-year-old male of European descent, is a dedicated teacher with over ten years of experience in his local high school. Recently married to Sarah, he has found himself struggling with intense and persistent feelings of anxiety and fear since an event that occurred three months ago. On the night of the incident, John was returning home from a late meeting at work. It was chilly and dark, with no one else around. As he walked down a dimly lit street, two individuals suddenly approached him from behind. One held a knife to his throat while the other demanded his wallet and phone. Despite complying without resistance, John was struck on the head several times before being left unconscious on the sidewalk. Since then, John's life has been marked by intrusive memories of the event. Flashbacks often occur when he is alone at home or during the night when everything is quiet. The sounds of sudden movement outside his window can jolt him back to that moment, reliving the terror and the sensation of the knife pressing against his throat. He feels a cold sweat break out across his skin as if it were happening again. At work, John has become increasingly hypervigilant, constantly scanning the hallways for signs of danger. The small noises in the school-like a door slamming or a sudden burst of laughter-are enough to send his heart racing and make him feel dizzy with anxiety. He often isolates himself from colleagues during breaks, finding their chatter overwhelming. John's sleep has been severely disrupted; he wakes up multiple times each night, drenched in sweat and feeling like he's suffocating. The recurring nightmares are relentless, replaying the mugging over and over again, leaving him exhausted and irritable throughout his workday. His patience with students seems to be waning; minor disruptions or tardiness now set off intense reactions of anger and frustration. In the classroom, John finds himself distracted by intrusive thoughts about his own safety and that of his colleagues and students. The anxiety is so palpable at times that he has trouble focusing on lesson plans or grading assignments. He often feels like he's in a constant state of alertness, which makes it hard to connect with his students emotionally or engage fully in teaching. His marriage has also been affected by these changes. Sarah notices John's increasing withdrawal and mood swings but struggles to understand why her attempts at support seem ineffective. Sometimes, she finds him pacing the house late into the night, muttering to himself about how he should have fought back or avoided the situation altogether. These thoughts consume his mind, causing a deep sense of guilt and self-blame. John has been trying to cope with his symptoms by avoiding certain areas of town where the mugging occurred, but even familiar places like grocery stores now trigger feelings of unease. He avoids going out alone at night and frequently checks that doors are locked securely before retiring for bed. Despite these challenges, John remains committed to teaching and supports Sarah in their efforts to start a family. His resilience is evident, yet the trauma continues to cast a long shadow over his daily life, making it difficult for him to return to the equilibrium he once knew.
